blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: Two API classes, SearchApi and ExportApi, both implement an interface that declares `Map<String, Integer> calls = new HashMap<>();` and a default method `allow(client)` that does `calls.merge(client, 1, Integer::sum) <= 3`. A client makes three calls through SearchApi and then its first call through ExportApi. What happens on that call?

options.text: It returns true, since every object that implements an interface carries its own copy of the interface's fields
options.says: an interface field is public static final: there is one map, and no object carries a copy

options.text: It returns false, since the field is static, so the calls made through SearchApi count for ExportApi as well
options.says: the interface's field is static, so ExportApi sees the three calls made through SearchApi and the fourth is refused

options.text: It fails to compile, since a default method can't change what a field of the interface holds
options.says: final forbids assigning the field; merge changes the map the field holds, and a mutable object in an interface field compiles

options.text: It throws UnsupportedOperationException, since a map held in a final field of an interface can't be changed
options.says: the field is final, not the map: the page's audit trail adds to its interface list without an error

origin.section: An Interface Can't Hold an Object's State: a Field Declared There Is One Constant for Every Implementation

questions.stem: An abstract class Report has a protected constructor `Report(String title)` that throws IllegalArgumentException for a blank title, and one abstract method, `abstract String body();`. A test in Report's package writes `Report r = new Report("  ") { String body() { return "x"; } };`. What happens?

options.text: It compiles, and the line throws IllegalArgumentException, since the anonymous class's constructor passes the title to Report's
options.says: an anonymous subclass's constructor, which javac writes, passes the argument to super(...), so Report's check runs

options.text: It compiles, and r is built with the blank title, since the anonymous class gets a constructor of its own that skips Report's check
options.says: the anonymous class's constructor, which javac writes, calls super(...) with the argument, so Report's check runs

options.text: It doesn't compile, since new can't be applied to a class declared abstract
options.says: abstract forbids new Report(...) itself; new Report(...) { ... } creates an anonymous subclass and compiles

options.text: It doesn't compile, since a protected constructor can't be called from a test in another class
options.says: a protected constructor is called by subclasses through super(...), and the anonymous class is a subclass

origin.section: An Abstract Class Can't Be Instantiated, but Its Constructor Runs for Every Subclass

questions.stem: Reporting library 2.0 adds an abstract method `void flush()` to its public Exporter interface. An application upgrades to 2.0 and recompiles its own code, which gets its Exporter from a vendor's factory and never names the vendor's CsvExporter class; CsvExporter was compiled against 1.x and knows nothing of flush(). The application runs a day of exports through CsvExporter, then calls flush() on it. What happens, and when?

options.text: Before the exports start, an error when CsvExporter is loaded, since the JVM checks a class against its interfaces as it links it
options.says: the class loads and links; that it lacks the method is found out only when the method is called

options.text: Before the exports start, a compile error when the application is rebuilt, since javac checks the implementations of the interface on the class path
options.says: the application's code names only Exporter, which it implements nowhere, so it compiles; only rebuilding CsvExporter itself would fail

options.text: At the flush() call, an error, since the class's missing method is found out only when that method is called
options.says: the old binary runs every other method; the first call to the new abstract method throws AbstractMethodError

options.text: At the flush() call, nothing at all, since the JVM gives an old class an empty body for a missing interface method
options.says: only a default method gives old classes a body; an abstract one leaves them throwing AbstractMethodError

origin.section: Adding an Abstract Method to a Published Interface Breaks Every Implementer; a Default Method Doesn't

questions.stem: An interface Parser declares `Object parse(String text);`, `String toString();` and a default method `parseOrNull(String text)` that calls parse. It has no annotation. Does `Parser p = text -> Integer.valueOf(text);` compile?

options.text: Yes, since parse is the only abstract method that the lambda must supply
options.says: toString is a public method of Object and the default has a body, so only parse counts

options.text: Yes, since a lambda may implement an interface with any number of abstract methods
options.says: a lambda needs exactly one abstract method that isn't a public method of Object

options.text: No, since toString is declared abstract here and counts as a second method to supply
options.says: public methods of Object don't count: every object already has toString

options.text: No, since the interface lacks @FunctionalInterface and so can't be the target of a lambda
options.says: the annotation only makes javac check the interface; one abstract method is enough without it

origin.section: A Functional Interface Is the Lightest Abstraction: One Abstract Method, and Any Lambda Implements It

concepts: A default method gives old implementations a body, so they keep running and still compile.

An interface with exactly one abstract method, not counting public methods of Object, is functional with or without @FunctionalInterface; the annotation makes javac reject a second abstract method at the interface.
Adding an abstract method to a published interface makes implementers fail to compile when rebuilt, and old binaries throw AbstractMethodError at the first call of the method.
